facts.content: That's in the same units of account. I invest the same today, $1, and I get dollars tomorrow. The change rate (exchange rate) for tomorrow must be considered. If the UK bond yields 10% and the US bond yields 5%, the higher nominal return does not guarantee a better investment. A 5% higher bond return can be erased by a 5% depreciation of the foreign currency. If the pound is expected to depreciate relative to the dollar, investing in the UK bond may lose value when converted back. If the dollar is expected to appreciate 5% relative to the pound, the investor is indifferent between the two bonds. US bond yields 5% next year. UK bond yields 10% but incurs a 5% capital loss due to dollar appreciation. Net return from both US and UK bonds is 5% when exchange-rate effects are accounted for. In integrated markets, returns on equivalent assets should be similar in equilibrium. Equilibrium requires the two investment returns to be equal.

evidence.quote: That's in the same units of account.
I invest the same today, $1, and I get dollars tomorrow.

And as you correctly pointed out, this thing here,
 therefore, requires that you sort of think about what
 the change rate is likely to be tomorrow.

So for example, in my example here, when I said,
 suppose i is 5%, and i star interest rate in the UK
 bond is 10%, is it obvious that I should invest in the UK bond?

And the answer is no, not so fast,
 because I know I'm going to make 5% more in terms
 of the return of the bond.

But then when I convert it back to dollar,
 I may lose all that gain because the pound has depreciated
 vis-a-vis the dollar.

In particular, if the pound, I expect the pound
 to depreciate relative to dollar.

Or if I expect the dollar to appreciate relative to the pound
 by 5%, then I'm indifferent.

If I go the UK bond route, I get 10% in return in the bond, minus 5% in the capital loss
 due to the appreciation of the dollar.
So net I get 5% as well.

So what I did here is say, you know, if the markets are very integrated and they function
 fairly well, those two returns should be more or less similar in equilibrium because
 prices are going to adjust, exchanges are going to adjust, and so on.

But in equilibrium, you have to find that equilibrium,
 these two things are going to be equal.
